questions.learningObjective: Explain why a cache-timing measurement flushes between attempts
questions.stem: A revision group writes a note explaining why a cache-timing measurement flushes the cache between attempts.

answer.exemplar: The note should say that the measurement works by checking whether a particular address is still present in the cache, and that a leftover entry from the previous attempt would look exactly like a hit in the current one, so the reader would be reading the old result rather than the new state. questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What makes a fixed-time comparison safe
questions.learningObjective: Give guidance for writing a timing-resistant comparison
questions.stem: A revision group drafts guidance for writing a comparison routine that resists timing attacks.

answer.exemplar: The guidance should say that the routine must do the same work for every input, so the loop must not stop early at the first difference, that each byte must still be compared and the result folded into an accumulator, and that the accumulator must be read only at the end. It should also say that a short-circuit check such as a length test, a string library call or a compiler optimisation that skips the comparison can put the timing signal back, so the compiled result should be checked as well as the source.

questions.explanation: A resistant routine does the same work for every input: no early exit, every byte compared, and the result read at the end. Short-circuit checks or optimisations can reintroduce the timing signal.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the corruptions only a shadow stack detected
questions.stem: A study group counts 150 simulated return address corruptions, of which a canary detected 96 and a shadow stack detected 135.
questions.explanation: 135 minus 96 is 39 corruptions that only the shadow stack detected, and those are the cases where the canary was overwritten along with the return address. A second copy elsewhere covers that slice.
questions.hint: Subtract the two detection totals.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What running a network service unprivileged buys
questions.learningObjective: Read an incident note to see what an account boundary contained

stimulus.body: The note records that an exploited parsing service was used to read files outside its own directory. It also records that the account running the service had no privilege to reach the configuration of any other service.

questions.stem: What does the incident note show about the account the service ran under?

options.text: The account's narrow rights limited what the attacker could reach, which is the point of running unprivileged.
The account's rights were irrelevant, because the attacker used the service's own code to read the files.
options.misconception: dismisses the value of the account boundary

options.text: The account should have been given more rights, because a narrow account slows down legitimate requests.
options.misconception: prioritises performance over isolation

options.text: The note shows the account was still privileged, because reading configuration files needs privilege.
options.misconception: assumes reading config needs privilege

questions.explanation: The account's narrow rights decided how far the attacker could get, because every read was subject to what the account could access. The same code under a privileged account would reach much further.
questions.hint: Ask what the account's rights limited.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a timing difference in a comparison leaks
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a byte-by-byte timing leak reveals over repeated attempts
questions.stem: The revision group measures a check that compares a supplied value against a stored secret, one byte at a time.

options.text: The check leaks the position of the first matching byte, and repeated measurements recover the secret.
The check leaks nothing, because the attacker has to send the whole value for the comparison to happen.
options.misconception: assumes guessing is not enough

options.text: The check leaks only whether the whole value matched, because the result is the only thing returned.
options.misconception: assumes only the result is observable

options.text: The check leaks the length of the secret, but not its contents, because the loop runs once per byte.
options.misconception: confuses loop count with a length leak

questions.explanation: First read the timing: the check returns sooner when the first byte differs, so the first match position is exposed. Repeat it: knowing where it stopped reveals that byte, and the next follows.
questions.hint: Read what the early return gives away.
